title: Doom for Nineveh, Relief for Judah
overview: Nahum announces that the LORD will bring down Nineveh, capital of the brutal Assyrian empire, and free Judah from its grip.

parts.label: A message against Nineveh (v. 1)
parts.note: The opening calls this a heavy message aimed at Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed northern Israel and long dominated Judah. Nothing is known about Nahum himself, and scholars are unsure where his hometown, Elkosh, was.

parts.label: God as a mighty storm (vv. 2-6)
parts.note: Calling God jealous here means he is fiercely protective of his people and will not let their oppressors go unpunished, and his patience is described as restraint, not weakness. The images of drying seas, shaking mountains and withering Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon, which were famous for pasture, farmland and forests, say that nothing on earth can stand against him.

parts.label: Shelter and flood (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: The same God is pictured as a safe stronghold for those who trust him and an overwhelming flood for Nineveh. Some readers see a hint of how the city actually fell in 612 BC, possibly with help from flooding, though that link is uncertain.

parts.label: Assyria's schemes will fail (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: Assyria's plans against the LORD will come to nothing, and its people are compared to tangled thorns thrown into a fire and to drunkards who fall at a touch. The plotter in verse 11 is not named; many think of an Assyrian king such as Sennacherib, who invaded Judah, but that is a guess.

parts.label: Chains broken, a grave dug (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: God tells Judah that its suffering under Assyria is ending, picturing the empire as a yoke and chains about to be snapped. Nineveh, by contrast, is told it will lose its name, the statues of its gods and its future.

parts.label: Good news on the mountains (v. 15)
parts.note: A runner crosses the hills announcing peace, so Judah can again hold its festivals and keep its promises to God without fear of invasion. Isaiah 52:7 uses nearly the same words, and Christians later read this image as a picture of the message about Jesus.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read this chapter's picture of an avenging God alongside Jesus' call to love enemies, some seeing it as just judgment on real cruelty and others as the honest cry of an oppressed people that later Scripture reframes.
think: When a cruel and powerful force finally falls, is it right to feel glad about it, and where do you think justice ends and revenge begins?
